claim: Vulnerability to noise-induced tinnitus is associated with increased spontaneous firing rate in dorsal cochlear nucleus principal neurons, fusiform cells.
source: Vulnerability to noise-induced tinnitus is associated with increased spontaneous firing rate in dorsal cochlear nucleus principal neurons, fusiform cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Zhang and Kaltenbach, 1998; Brozoski et al., 2002; Li et al., 2013) as referenced in the Introduction section.

claim: Hyperactivity in fusiform cells is caused, at least in part, by decreased Kv7.2/3 (KCNQ2/3) potassium currents.
source: This hyperactivity is caused, at least in part, by decreased Kv7.2/3 (KCNQ2/3) potassium currents.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Li et al., 2013) as referenced in the Introduction and Results sections.

claim: Noise exposure induces, on average, a reduction in KCNQ2/3 channel activity in fusiform cells in noise-exposed mice by 4 days after exposure.
source: Our results show that noise exposure induces, on average, a reduction in KCNQ2/3 channel activity in fusiform cells in noise-exposed mice by 4 days after exposure.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B showing reduced KCNQ2/3 current amplitude in 4 days noise-exposed mice compared to 4 days sham-exposed mice.

claim: Tinnitus is developed in mice that do not compensate for the reduction in KCNQ2/3 channel activity within 3 days after the initial reduction.
source: Tinnitus is developed in mice that do not compensate for this reduction within the next 3 days.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing that mice with persistent KCNQ2/3 reduction at 7 days develop tinnitus, while those that recover do not.

claim: Resilience to tinnitus is developed in mice that show a re-emergence of KCNQ2/3 channel activity and a reduction in HCN channel activity.
source: Resilience to tinnitus is developed in mice that show a re-emergence of KCNQ2/3 channel activity and a reduction in HCN channel activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing normal KCNQ2/3 currents and reduced HCN channel activity in non-tinnitus mice at 7 days post-exposure (Figures 5B and Li et al., 2013).

claim: 52.4% (11/21) of noise-exposed mice exhibited a significant gap detection deficit at high-frequency (20–32 kHz) but not at low-frequency (10–16 kHz) background sounds 7 days after noise exposure.
source: Our results showed that 7 days after noise exposure, 52.4% (11/21) of the noise-exposed mice exhibited a significant gap detection deficit at high-frequency (20–32 kHz) but not at low-frequency (10–16 kHz) background sounds.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Prepulse inhibition (PPI) was similar among control, tinnitus, and non-tinnitus mice.
source: prepulse inhibition, PPI, was similar among control, tinnitus, and non-tinnitus mice (Figure 1A bottom left, diagram showing startle-only and prepulse trials; Figure 1A bottom middle and right, representative startle responses from control, tinnitus and non-tinnitus mice; Figure 1C, summary graphs of PPI ratio; Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–G, 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–G.

claim: Tinnitus and non-tinnitus mice displayed similar hearing thresholds before and after noise-exposure, as evidenced by their similar auditory brainstem response (ABR) thresholds.
source: Moreover, tinnitus and non-tinnitus mice displayed similar hearing thresholds before and after noise-exposure, as evidenced by their similar auditory brainstem response (ABR) thresholds (Figure 2A,B; 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Tinnitus and non-tinnitus mice showed no differences in wave I amplitude, suggesting no difference in the damage of afferent nerve terminals between these two groups.
source: Whereas wave I amplitudes were reduced after noise-exposure for all noise-exposed mice, tinnitus and non-tinnitus mice showed no differences in wave I amplitude, suggesting no difference in the damage of afferent nerve terminals between these two groups (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Ablation of the DCN 3–5 months after the acoustic trauma did not affect the psychophysical evidence of tinnitus.
source: Ablation of the DCN 3–5 months after the acoustic trauma did not affect the psychophysical evidence of tinnitus (Brozoski and Bauer, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Brozoski and Bauer, 2005.

claim: When bilateral DCN lesion occurred prior to noise exposure, it prevented the induction of tinnitus.
source: However, when bilateral DCN lesion occurred prior to noise exposure, it prevented the induction of tinnitus (Brozoski et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Brozoski et al., 2012.

claim: DCN is not essential for the maintenance of tinnitus, but it is indispensable for the induction of tinnitus.
source: These results suggest that although DCN is not essential for the maintenance of tinnitus, it is indispensable for the induction of tinnitus.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cited studies (Brozoski and Bauer, 2005; Brozoski et al., 2012) showing differential effects of DCN lesions depending on timing.

claim: Fusiform cell hyperactivity in tinnitus mice is associated with reduced KCNQ2/3 currents at hyperpolarized membrane potentials, due to a depolarizing shift in the voltage dependence of KCNQ2/3 channel opening.
source: Importantly, fusiform cell hyperactivity in tinnitus mice is associated with reduced KCNQ2/3 currents at hyperpolarized membrane potentials, due to a depolarizing shift in the voltage dependence of KCNQ2/3 channel opening (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Li et al., 2013.

claim: Non-tinnitus mice do not show fusiform cell hyperactivity after sound exposure and express normal levels of KCNQ2/3 currents.
source: On the other hand, non-tinnitus mice do not show fusiform cell hyperactivity after sound exposure and express normal levels of KCNQ2/3 currents (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Li et al., 2013.

claim: 4 days noise-exposed mice showed a significant reduction in KCNQ2/3 current amplitude.
source: 4 days noise-exposed mice showed a significant reduction in KCNQ2/3 current amplitude (Figure 3B; 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The Gmax of KCNQ2/3 currents was not different between 4 days sham- and 4 days noise-exposed mice.
source: A Boltzmann fit of the KCNQ2/3 conductance–voltage (G–V) function showed that the Gmax of KCNQ2/3 currents was not different between 4 days sham- and 4 days noise-exposed mice (Figure 3C,E)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C,E.

claim: The V1/2 of KCNQ2/3 channels was shifted to more depolarized potentials in the 4 days noise-exposed mice.
source: but the V1/2 was shifted to more depolarized potentials in the 4 days noise-exposed mice (Figure 3C,D; 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: The reduction of KCNQ2/3 currents in 4 days noise-exposed mice is due, at least in part, to a depolarizing shift in the V1/2 of KCNQ2/3 channels.
source: These results suggest that the reduction of KCNQ2/3 currents in 4 days noise-exposed mice is due, at least in part, to a depolarizing shift in the V1/2 of KCNQ2/3 channels, which is mechanistically similar to the reduction of KCNQ2/3 currents in tinnitus mice when assessed 7 days after noise exposure (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3C,D and comparison to previous findings (Li et al., 2013).

claim: Application of retigabine at day 4 significantly reduced the percentage of mice that developed tinnitus.
source: Application of retigabine at day 4 significantly reduced the percentage of mice that developed tinnitus (Figure 3F; 'Materials and methods')
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The recovery of KCNQ2/3 currents between day 4 and 7 is crucial for tinnitus resilience.
source: suggesting that the recovery of KCNQ2/3 currents between day 4 and 7 is crucial for tinnitus resilience.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental finding that retigabine application starting at day 4 reduces tinnitus incidence (Figure 3F).

claim: Experience-dependent bidirectional plasticity of KCNQ2/3 channel activity is associated with the vulnerability and resilience to noise-induced tinnitus.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that experience-dependent bidirectional plasticity of KCNQ2/3 channel activity is associated with the vulnerability and resilience to noise-induced tinnitus: experience-dependent depression in KCNQ2/3 channel activity is important for vulnerability, while experience-dependent recovery in KCNQ2/3 channel activity is important for resilience to tinnitus.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined experimental data showing reduction at 4 days, persistence in tinnitus mice, and recovery in non-tinnitus mice.

claim: Fusiform cells from non-tinnitus mice showed more hyperpolarized resting membrane potential (RMP) compared to control mice.
source: When we blocked fusiform cell spontaneous firing activity with tetrodotoxin (0.5 μM, a specific sodium channel blocker), we found that fusiform cells from non-tinnitus mice showed more hyperpolarized resting membrane potential (RMP; Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Fusiform cell RMP is similar between control and tinnitus mice.
source: Because fusiform cell RMP is similar between control and tinnitus mice (Li et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Li et al., 2013.

claim: Onset Rin was not different among control, tinnitus, and non-tinnitus mice.
source: Moreover, when we used small current steps to evaluate the onset and steady state input resistance (Rin; Figure 4D; 'Materials and methods'), we found that onset Rin was not different among control, tinnitus, and non-tinnitus mice (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Non-tinnitus mice displayed a significantly increased steady-state Rin compared to control and tinnitus mice.
source: However, non-tinnitus mice displayed a significantly increased steady-state Rin, which was revealed later in the voltage response (Figure 4C; 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Fusiform cells from non-tinnitus mice exhibit a decrease in a slowly activating and deactivating depolarizing conductance that is open at subthreshold potentials.
source: Together, our results revealed that fusiform cells from non-tinnitus mice exhibit a decrease in a slowly activating and deactivating depolarizing conductance that is open at subthreshold potentials.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental findings of hyperpolarized RMP and increased steady-state Rin in non-tinnitus mice.

claim: Fusiform cells from non-tinnitus mice showed significantly reduced HCN channel activity compared to control and tinnitus mice.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, fusiform cells from non-tinnitus mice showed significantly reduced HCN channel activity (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: ZD7288 application abolished the differences in steady-state input resistance and in RMP among control, tinnitus, and non-tinnitus mice.
source: Indeed, ZD7288 application abolished the differences in steady-state input resistance and in RMP among control, tinnitus, and non-tinnitus mice (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C–E.

claim: Reduced HCN channel activity is a major contributor for the more hyperpolarized RMP and increased steady-state Rin in non-tinnitus mice.
source: Together, our results are consistent with the notion that reduced HCN channel activity is a major contributor for the more hyperpolarized RMP and increased steady-state Rin in non-tinnitus mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that ZD7288 (HCN blocker) abolishes the differences in RMP and steady-state Rin (Figure 5C–E).

claim: Noise-induced reduction in HCN channel activity is a critical biophysical change associated with resilience to tinnitus.
source: Moreover, our results show that noise-induced reduction in HCN channel activity is another critical biophysical change associated with resilience to tinnitus.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced HCN activity specifically in non-tinnitus mice (Figure 5B).

claim: HCN channel activity was not different between sham-exposed and noise-exposed mice 4 days after noise exposure.
source: Our results revealed that although noise-exposed mice showed significantly reduced KCNQ2/3 currents in fusiform cells 4 days after noise exposure (Figure 3B), HCN channel activity was not different between sham-exposed and noise-exposed mice (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: The decrease in KCNQ2/3 activity happens before the reduction of HCN channel activity.
source: These results indicate that the decrease in KCNQ2/3 activity happens before the reduction of HCN channel activity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the temporal sequence of changes: KCNQ2/3 reduction at 4 days (Figure 3B) but no HCN change at 4 days (Figure 6B), with HCN reduction appearing by 7 days (Figure 5B).

claim: Fusiform cells from retigabine-injected mice displayed reduced HCN channel activity.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, we found that fusiform cells from retigabine-injected mice, which showed reduced incidence of tinnitus and reduced spontaneous firing rate of fusiform cells (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,C,D), displayed reduced HCN channel activity (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Application of KCNQ channel activators did not affect ABR thresholds, wave I amplitude, or PPI ratios.
source: Moreover, application of KCNQ channel activators did not affect ABR thresholds, wave I amplitude, or PPI ratios (Figure 7B–D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B–D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Application of retigabine does not have any effect on hearing thresholds.
source: These results are consistent with recent studies showing that application of retigabine does not have any effect on hearing thresholds (Sheppard et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sheppard et al., 2015.

claim: Application of retigabine reduced hearing loss in an animal model of sodium salicylate-induced sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus.
source: However, application of retigabine reduced hearing loss in an animal model of sodium salicylate-induced sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus (Sheppard et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sheppard et al., 2015.

claim: Increases in KCNQ2/3 channel activity promote a decrease in fusiform cell HCN channel activity and resilience to tinnitus.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that increases in KCNQ2/3 channel activity promote a decrease in fusiform cell HCN channel activity and resilience to tinnitus.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that retigabine (KCNQ activator) reduces HCN activity (Figure 6C,D) and tinnitus incidence (Figure 7A).

claim: 4 days noise-exposed mice showed normal fusiform cell spontaneous firing activity and no behavioral evidence of tinnitus.
source: Surprisingly, 4 days noise-exposed mice showed normal fusiform cell spontaneous firing activity and no behavioral evidence of tinnitus (Figure 8A,B, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A,B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fusiform cells from 4 days noise-exposed mice showed hyperpolarized RMP.
source: The lack of association between reduced KCNQ2/3 channel activity and fusiform cell hyperactivity may be explained by the hyperpolarized RMP in fusiform cells from 4 days noise-exposed mice (Figure 8C)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Biophysical changes that are associated with increases in fusiform cell spontaneous firing rates lead to tinnitus, while biophysical changes that maintain normal levels of spontaneous firing rates are associated with tinnitus resilience.
source: These results suggest that biophysical changes that are associated with increases in fusiform cell spontaneous firing rates lead to tinnitus, while biophysical changes that maintain normal levels of spontaneous firing rates are associated with tinnitus resilience.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that 4 days noise-exposed mice have reduced KCNQ2/3 but normal firing rates and no tinnitus, while 7 days tinnitus mice have reduced KCNQ2/3, increased firing rates, and tinnitus.

claim: Gap detection deficits in noise-exposed mice were evident only when the gap was placed immediately, but not 80 ms, before the startle stimulus.
source: However, the interpretation that tinnitus 'fills in' the gap in the background sound that precedes the startle stimulus is not compatible with a recent study, which showed that gap detection deficits in noise-exposed mice were evident only when the gap was placed immediately, but not 80 ms, before the startle stimulus (Hickox and Liberman, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hickox and Liberman, 2014.

claim: Human studies revealed gap detection deficits in tinnitus sufferers, but the frequency of the tinnitus percept did not fully match the frequency of the background sound where gap detection deficits were observed.
source: Moreover, although human studies revealed gap detection deficits in tinnitus sufferers, which are consistent with the use of the gap detection in animal studies, the frequency of the tinnitus percept did not fully match the frequency of the background sound where gap detection deficits were observed (Fournier and Hebert, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fournier and Hebert, 2013.

claim: Other human studies, which used higher-level cognitive tasks but not the acoustic reflex for assessing gap detection, did not reveal gap detection deficits in tinnitus sufferers.
source: Other human studies, which used higher-level cognitive tasks but not the acoustic reflex for assessing gap detection, did not reveal gap detection deficits in tinnitus sufferers (Campolo et al., 2013; Boyen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Campolo et al., 2013 and Boyen et al., 2015.

claim: KCNQ2/3 channels are slowly activating, non-inactivating voltage-dependent potassium channels that are open at hyperpolarized (subthreshold) voltages.
source: KCNQ2/3 channels are slowly activating, non-inactivating voltage-dependent potassium channels that are open at hyperpolarized (subthreshold) voltages.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about KCNQ2/3 channel biophysics.

claim: KCNQ2/3 channels control subthreshold membrane potential and serve as a powerful brake of neuronal firing activity.
source: As a result, they control subthreshold membrane potential and serve as a powerful brake of neuronal firing activity (Maljevic et al., 2008; Brown and Passmore, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Maljevic et al., 2008 and Brown and Passmore, 2009.

claim: Disorders that are characterized by neuronal hyperexcitability, such as epilepsy, neuropathic pain, and tinnitus are linked to genetic or experience-dependent reductions in KCNQ2/3 channel activity.
source: Disorders that are characterized by neuronal hyperexcitability, such as epilepsy, neuropathic pain, and tinnitus are linked to genetic or experience-dependent reductions in KCNQ2/3 channel activity (Biervert et al., 1998; Dedek et al., 2001; Kullmann, 2002; Wuttke et al., 2007; Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Biervert et al., 1998; Dedek et al., 2001; Kullmann, 2002; Wuttke et al., 2007; Li et al., 2013).

claim: Pharmacological activation of KCNQ channels by retigabine or by SF0034 prevent seizures, neuropathic pain and the development of tinnitus.
source: Pharmacological activation of KCNQ channels by retigabine, an FDA approved anti-epileptic drug that activates KCNQ2-5, or by SF0034, a potent KCNQ2/3 activator, prevent seizures, neuropathic pain and the development of tinnitus (Gunthorpe et al., 2012; Li et al., 2013; Kalappa et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gunthorpe et al., 2012; Li et al., 2013; and Kalappa et al., 2015.

claim: KCNQ2/3 channel activity is plastic and can be enhanced in response to increased neuronal activity.
source: Because in vitro studies have shown that KCNQ2/3 channel activity is plastic and can be enhanced in response to increased neuronal activity (Wu et al., 2008; Brown and Randall, 2009; Misonou, 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wu et al., 2008; Brown and Randall, 2009; and Misonou, 2010.

claim: KCNQ2/3 channels mediate the native neuronal M-type current.
source: KCNQ2/3 channels mediate the native neuronal M-type current (Wang et al., 1998)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 1998.

claim: M-type current is a slowly activating voltage-gated potassium current blocked by muscarinic acetylcholine (M) receptors.
source: a slowly activating voltage-gated potassium current blocked by muscarinic acetylcholine (M) receptors (Brown and Adams, 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Brown and Adams, 1980.

claim: KCNQ2/3 currents are strongly inhibited by activation of G protein-coupled receptors that reduce membrane phosphatidylinositol-(4,5)-bisphosphate (PIP2) levels.
source: KCNQ2/3 currents are strongly inhibited not only by activation of M receptors, but also by activation of other G protein-coupled receptors that reduce membrane phosphatidylinositol-(4,5)-bisphosphate (PIP2) levels, which is the major determinant in KCNQ channel gating (Marrion, 1997; Zhang et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Marrion, 1997 and Zhang et al., 2003.

claim: Noise exposure increases basal cholinergic activity in the DCN.
source: Importantly, because noise exposure increases basal cholinergic activity in the DCN (Jin et al., 2006; Kaltenbach and Zhang, 2007; Manzoor et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jin et al., 2006; Kaltenbach and Zhang, 2007; and Manzoor et al., 2013.

claim: Noise-induced increases and decreases in basal M receptor signaling may underlie the bidirectional plasticity of KCNQ2/3 channel activity.
source: we propose that noise-induced increases and decreases (or recovery to baseline levels) in basal (tonic) M receptor signaling may underlie the bidirectional plasticity of KCNQ2/3 channel activity.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the known relationship between M receptors and KCNQ channels and the observed changes in cholinergic activity after noise exposure.

claim: HCN channels are non-inactivating cation channels that open at hyperpolarized voltages.
source: HCN channels are non-inactivating cation channels that open at hyperpolarized voltages.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about HCN channel biophysics.

claim: HCN channels depolarize the RMP and reduce membrane resistance, thereby stabilizing the membrane voltage by opposing its alterations in response to synaptic inputs.
source: Because of their voltage-dependent properties and their reversal potential at −30 mV, HCN channels not only depolarize the RMP, but also reduce membrane resistance and therefore stabilize the membrane voltage by opposing its alterations in response to synaptic inputs (Pape, 1996; Robinson and Siegelbaum, 2003; Biel et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pape, 1996; Robinson and Siegelbaum, 2003; and Biel et al., 2009.

claim: Changes in HCN channel activity affect intrinsic and synaptic excitability in opposing directions.
source: Therefore, changes in HCN channel activity affect intrinsic and synaptic excitability in opposing directions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the known biophysical properties of HCN channels.

claim: HCN plasticity has been implicated in the vulnerability and resilience to several neurological disorders characterized by abnormal synaptic or intrinsic excitability, such as epilepsy, neuropathic pain, depression, and Parkinson's disease.
source: This differential influence of HCN channels on synaptic and intrinsic neuronal excitability has implicated HCN plasticity in the vulnerability and resilience to several neurological disorders characterized by abnormal synaptic or intrinsic excitability, such as epilepsy, neuropathic pain, depression, and Parkinson's disease (Chaplan et al., 2003; Biel et al., 2009; Chan et al., 2011; Emery et al., 2011; Friedman et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chaplan et al., 2003; Biel et al., 2009; Chan et al., 2011; Emery et al., 2011; and Friedman et al., 2014.

claim: Reduction of HCN channel activity in non-tinnitus mice prevents fusiform cell hyperactivity and contributes to tinnitus resilience by hyperpolarizing the RMP of fusiform cell.
source: We suggest that reduced HCN channel activity in non-tinnitus mice prevents fusiform cell hyperactivity and contributes to tinnitus resilience by hyperpolarizing the RMP of fusiform cell (Figures 4 and 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 4 and 5 and represents an inference about the mechanism.

claim: Decreased HCN channel activity increased the steady-state Rin of fusiform cells, which is expected to enhance responsiveness of fusiform cells to synaptic inputs.
source: Moreover, decreased HCN channel activity increased the steady-state Rin of fusiform cells (Figures 4C and 5D), which is expected to enhance responsiveness of fusiform cells to synaptic inputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 4C and 5D and represents an inference about functional consequences.

claim: Reduction of HCN channel activity in fusiform cells may contribute to enhanced evoked activity and potentially to noise-induced hyperacusis.
source: Therefore, reduction of HCN channel activity in fusiform cells may contribute to enhanced evoked activity and potentially to noise-induced hyperacusis—the perception of moderate-level sounds as intolerably loud.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential consequences of reduced HCN activity.

claim: Large increases in postsynaptic calcium lead to enhancement in HCN current amplitude via NMDA receptor activation, CaMKII activation and increased HCN channel expression.
source: Previous studies have shown that large increases in postsynaptic calcium lead to enhancement in HCN current amplitude via NMDA receptor (NMDAR) activation, CaMKII activation and increased HCN channel expression (Fan et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fan et al., 2005.

claim: Smaller increases in calcium through L-type calcium channels and/or activation of mGluRs and PKC activation lead to activity-dependent decreases in HCN expression.
source: while smaller increases in calcium through L-type calcium channels and/or activation of mGluRs and PKC activation lead to activity-dependent decreases in HCN expression (Brager and Johnston, 2007; Chan et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brager and Johnston, 2007 and Chan et al., 2011.

claim: Pharmacological enhancement of KCNQ channels with retigabine reduces spontaneous firing rate in fusiform cells.
source: Pharmacological enhancement of KCNQ channels with retigabine reduces spontaneous firing rate in fusiform cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Decreases in spontaneous firing caused by enhancement in KCNQ2/3 channel activity may lead to changes in intracellular calcium, which may trigger a homeostatic mechanism that decreases HCN currents.
source: Therefore, we propose that decreases in spontaneous firing that may be caused by the enhancement in KCNQ2/3 channel activity lead to changes in intracellular calcium, which, in turn, may trigger a homeostatic mechanism that decreases HCN currents in an effort to normalize spontaneous spike rates.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal about the mechanism linking KCNQ enhancement to HCN reduction.

claim: The HCN2 subunit is expressed in fusiform cells that lack HCN1 subunit expression.
source: Immunohistochemical studies have shown that the HCN2 subunit is expressed in fusiform cells that lack HCN1 subunit expression (Koch et al., 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Koch et al., 2004.

claim: HCN2 isoforms may mediate the noise-induced plasticity in fusiform cells.
source: suggesting that HCN2 isoforms may mediate the noise-induced plasticity in fusiform cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression pattern of HCN subunits in fusiform cells.

claim: Manipulations that reduce HCN2 channel activity may serve as potential therapeutic path for preventing the development of tinnitus.
source: Therefore, we propose that manipulations that reduce HCN2 channel activity may serve as potential therapeutic path for preventing the development of tinnitus.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal about potential therapeutic approaches.

claim: Noise-induced increases in Kirs may mediate the hyperpolarization of RMP at 4 days post-exposure and hence resilience to tinnitus.
source: Because various levels of inwardly rectifying potassium channels (Kir) set the diverse RMP of fusiform cells (Leao et al., 2012), we suggest that noise-induced increases in Kirs may mediate this hyperpolarization of RMP and hence resilience to tinnitus.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion based on the known role of Kir channels in setting RMP.

claim: Reduction in KCNQ2/3 channel activity is a robust mechanism for triggering tinnitus, but its pathogenic effect is gated by the RMP of fusiform cells.
source: We conclude that reduction in KCNQ2/3 channel activity is a robust mechanism for triggering tinnitus, but its pathogenic effect is gated by the RMP of fusiform cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that reduced KCNQ2/3 at 4 days does not cause tinnitus when RMP is hyperpolarized, but does cause tinnitus at 7 days when RMP is normal.

claim: Manipulations that hyperpolarize the fusiform cell RMP may provide additional therapeutic approaches for preventing tinnitus.
source: Therefore, besides targeting KCNQ2/3 channel activators for preventing tinnitus, manipulations that hyperpolarize the fusiform cell RMP may also provide additional therapeutic approaches.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal about potential therapeutic approaches.

claim: Similar neuronal output can result from multiple combinations of intrinsic and synaptic properties.
source: These findings complement and extend previous experimental and theoretical work showing that similar neuronal output can result from multiple combinations of intrinsic and synaptic properties (Edelman and Gally, 2001; Prinz et al., 2004; Marder and Goaillard, 2006; Goaillard and Dufour, 2014; Ratte et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Edelman and Gally, 2001; Prinz et al., 2004; Marder and Goaillard, 2006; Goaillard and Dufour, 2014; and Ratte et al., 2014.

claim: Activity-dependent changes in conductances that affect neuronal excitability frequently trigger homeostatic, compensatory changes in different conductances, which result in constant neuronal output.
source: In accordance with this view, activity-dependent changes in conductances that affect neuronal excitability frequently trigger homeostatic, compensatory changes in different conductances, which result in constant neuronal output (Desai et al., 1999; LeMasson et al., 1993; O'Leary et al., 2010; O'Leary et al., 2013; O'Leary et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Desai et al., 1999; LeMasson et al., 1993; O'Leary et al., 2010; O'Leary et al., 2013; and O'Leary et al., 2014.

claim: Homeostatic and coordinated regulation of potassium and HCN currents occurs in different species and neuronal circuits.
source: Because homeostatic and coordinated regulation of potassium and HCN currents occurs in different species and neuronal circuits, such as dopaminergic neurons in rat susbstantia nigra pars compact, neurons of the lobster stomatogastric ganglion and octopus and MSO auditory brainstem neurons (MacLean et al., 2003; Oertel et al., 2008; Khurana et al., 2011; Amendola et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to MacLean et al., 2003; Oertel et al., 2008; Khurana et al., 2011; and Amendola et al., 2012.

claim: Coordinated plasticity of potassium and HCN channels may represent a general biophysical strategy for achieving neuronal homeostasis.
source: we propose that coordinated plasticity of potassium and HCN channels may represent a general biophysical strategy for achieving neuronal homeostasis.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the observed patterns across different neuronal systems.

claim: A combination of drugs that enhance KCNQ2/3 and reduce HCN channel activity represents a potent therapeutic approach that will enhance resilience and reduce vulnerability to tinnitus.
source: Similarly, because plasticity of multiple conductances is involved in tinnitus, we propose that a combination of drugs that enhance KCNQ2/3 and reduce HCN channel activity represents a potent therapeutic approach that will enhance resilience and reduce vulnerability to tinnitus.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal about potential therapeutic approaches based on the findings.

claim: Simultaneous pharmacological enhancement of KCNQ2/3 and reduction of HCN channel activity is expected to act synergistically in stabilizing spontaneous firing rates in fusiform cells.
source: Moreover, simultaneous pharmacological enhancement of KCNQ2/3 and reduction of HCN channel activity is expected to act synergistically in stabilizing spontaneous firing rates in fusiform cells.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the expected effects of combined drug treatment.

claim: The synergistic effect of combined KCNQ2/3 enhancement and HCN reduction may reduce the required concentration for each individual drug to exert its effect and therefore may lead to increased potency and reduced toxicity.
source: This synergistic effect may in turn reduce the required concentration for each individual drug to exert its effect and therefore may lead to increased potency and reduced toxicity.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential benefits of combination therapy.
